news.title: US Munitions Sent to Ukraine Compared to Iran War as Trump Blames Biden
news.text: President Donald Trump has defended the costly dent the war on Iran has put in U.S. coffers and arms stockpiles by claiming that weapons production could be maintained indefinitely and blaming his predecessor for devoting even more munitions to Ukraine in its battle with Russia. "We have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place," Trump wrote Thursday on Truth Social. "In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before. We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen. We are taking them for ourselves, the U.S.A., rather than selling them to others, but the sales to Allies will soon again, begin. "Also, please let it be known, that the Biden Administration gave far more Munitions away to Ukraine, at no cost to them, whatsoever, than we have used in Iran," he continued. "Hundreds of Billions of Dollars was given to Ukraine and NATO, free of charge, that Europe would have paid for — If they were only asked, but we will be asking for that money, though somewhat belatedly!" But the reality of comparing U.S. commitments to two wars launched roughly four years apart and carrying different demands for Washington is more complex. And analysts argue the strain on the U.S. defense industrial base is real, leaving Washington and its partners potentially exposed. "It is clear that the United States is increasingly overstretched between these two conflicts," Christopher Chivvis, a former U.S. intelligence official serving today as senior fellow and director of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace's American Statecraft Program, told Newsweek. "This creates windows of opportunity for adversaries, including China and Russia, to exploit." "Trump’s statement that U.S. capacity is 'virtually unlimited' sounds fictional for any relevant time horizon," Chivvis said. "He may criticize the Biden administration for excessive support to Ukraine, but his decision to go to war with Iran has made the situation far worse, including by sapping the military of advanced precision munitions that it needs to deter a PLA invasion of Taiwan." Newsweek reached out to the Department of War for comment, but did not hear back in time for publication. In July, however, Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement shared with Newsweek for a similar story, “America’s military is the most powerful in the world and has everything it needs to execute at the time and place of the President’s choosing. We have executed multiple successful operations across combatant commands while ensuring the U.S. military possesses a deep arsenal of capabilities to protect our people and our interests." More Weapons for Ukraine, Higher Costs for Iran From Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine to the end of former President Joe Biden's administration in January 2025, the U.S. committed roughly $66 billion in security assistance, with around $130 billion more devoted to other forms of aid, according to the Department of Defense, later renamed the Department of War under Trump. How Many (and What Kind of) Weapons Did the US Send to Ukraine? Weapons provided include more than 4 million artillery shells, hundreds of thousands of mortar rounds, tens of thousands of rockets, and thousands of missiles and precision weapons. The U.S. also sent over 40 High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS), 12 National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems (NASAMS), and three Patriot batteries, along with their respective munitions. Other forms of U.S. military equipment include dozens of tanks, hundreds of other armored vehicles, around 20 helicopters and several other types of vehicles and support equipment. In the initial 39-day period of high-intensity hostilities launched against Iran following the start of the war in February 2026, the U.S. reportedly fired around 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles, 1,100 Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles (JASSM) and between 1,500 and 2,000 interceptors, including those used by Patriot, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) and Standard Missile (SM) systems, according to estimates by the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Significant numbers of other munitions such as Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAM), Small Diameter Bombs (SDB) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) were also fired. Meanwhile, the U.S. military is also believed to have lost more than 40 aviation assets, including dozens of drones and several fighter and cargo aircraft. Even accounting for additional munitions fired in subsequent rounds of conflict that have emerged in recent months, including the latest U.S. strikes conducted against targets in southern Iran on Wednesday, the raw total of weapons expended in the six-month conflict in the Middle East likely pales in comparison to arms transferred to Ukraine throughout four and a half years of war in Europe. What Weapons Are We Using in the Iran Conflict? But the raw number of weapons does not capture the strain on the U.S. arsenal. The Iran war has consumed some of the military's most expensive and strategically scarce precision and air-defense weapons at a far faster rate than the U.S. supplied them to Ukraine. For example, the price of a 155mm artillery shell is generally around $3,000–$4,000, while a single Tomahawk cruise missile costs roughly $2 million–$3 million. Patriot interceptors, more of which were reportedly fired in the first three days of the Iran war than had been provided to Ukraine over four years, are estimated to cost between $3 million and $4 million, with THAAD interceptors running up to $12 million per unit. Mark Montgomery, a retired U.S. rear admiral who serves as senior director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies' Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation, pointed out that "the vast majority" of U.S. weapons provided to Ukraine "has no crossover" with those expended in Iran. Montgomery told Newsweek that the rate of Patriot system involvement in the two wars was a specific area in which "the president is wrong" in his assessment, even if ultimately the U.S. "can continue both conflicts at the current pace for the foreseeable future." As for the total cost of the conflict, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth estimated in late July that the war in Iran had thus far cost the U.S. about $37.5 billion as the administration sought roughly $70 billion more in funds pertaining to operations. Adding in the effects of higher gas prices, costs of living, damage repairs and other factors, sources such as the Center for American Progress, the Iran War Ticker and Stephen Semler of Brown University's Cost of War project place the total price of the conflict above $100 billion. Americans Have Died in Both Wars The two conflicts also fundamentally differ for the U.S. in that one involves providing aid to a partner and the other a direct clash with a longtime foe. That divergence brings with it another kind of cost. Since the beginning of the war against Iran, the Pentagon has counted 18 U.S. service members killed in direct attacks or aircraft crashes. There have been no publicly acknowledged U.S. military personnel killed in combat in Ukraine, although a memorial in Kyiv lists 118 U.S. volunteers killed while fighting alongside the Ukrainian military. BBC News and Russian independent media outlet Mediazona have also counted three U.S. nationals killed while volunteering in support of Russia. But as Trump eschews new diplomatic inroads in favor of escalation against Iran, analysts fear the U.S. military death toll could rise in the face of dual battlefield demands. Jennifer Kavanagh, senior fellow and director of military analysis, argued that, even if "the United States has enough munitions to continue fighting in Iran for some time," particularly through limited strikes and the conversion of "dumb bombs" into precision weaponry through JDAM kits, "on the defensive side, it faces greater constraints." "It could protect U.S. forces against limited strikes for some time. However, it cannot meet these defensive needs and supply Ukraine with interceptors for the winter," Kavanagh told Newsweek. "And of course, continuing to expend weapons in Iran (and through aid to Ukraine however small) comes at a cost to future readiness and means it will be even longer before the United States is ready for another conflict." "Specifically, right now, the United States could not resource a major war with China or Russia," Kavanagh said. "The longer the war in Iran and aid to Ukraine continue, the longer the timeline before the U.S. military is once again prepared to defend the country against the most existential threats it might face." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: "The United States is increasingly overstretched between these two conflicts," a former U.S. intelligence official told Newsweek.

news.title: California girls’ sports advocates vow fight after judge tosses trans athlete case: 'Far from over'
news.text: Advocates for girls' sports vowed to keep fighting after a federal judge dismissed a Department of Justice lawsuit challenging California policies that allow biological male athletes to compete on girls' school sports teams. A DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital the administration remains committed to enforcing President Donald Trump’s policy barring biological males from girls’ sports despite the setback and is considering an appeal. "We are disappointed by the Court’s order, and remain committed to enforcing President Trump’s agenda preventing boys from playing in girls’ sports," the spokesperson said. "We are evaluating our options for appeal." Sophia Lorey, California Family Council outreach director and a former college soccer player who organized "Save Girls' Sports" demonstrations in California, told Fox News Digital that the ruling did not resolve what she called the central Title IX dispute. NEWSOM FACES CRITICISM FOR STATE'S STANCE ON TRANS ATHLETES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AFTER SCOTUS RULING "California should not mistake a courtroom technicality for a victory," she said. "The judge did not rule that allowing males into girls’ sports is fair, lawful, or consistent with Title IX. This case was dismissed on a technical issue without ever deciding the fundamental question at the heart of this fight." The court avoided the underlying debate over biological fairness entirely. Instead, U.S. District Judge Cynthia Valenzuela grounded her decision in administrative funding rules, finding that the federal government failed to give California explicit prior notice before threatening to pull $44 billion in education funds. The Justice Department sued the California Department of Education (CADOE) and California Interscholastic Federation (CIF) in July 2025, alleging their transgender athlete policies discriminated against female athletes. "I hope to see this decision appealed, but regardless, this fight is far from over," Lorey continued. "California lawmakers have the power right now to protect female athletes. A courtroom technicality does not erase biological sex, and it does not make discrimination against girls acceptable. We will not stop until CA girls are protected…California girls are still paying the price, losing medals, opportunities, roster spots, and privacy while state leaders prioritize gender identity over biological reality." NEWSOM'S OFFICE RESPONDS TO SCOTUS RULING ON WOMEN'S SPORTS AS CALIFORNIA FACES ONGOING TRANS ATHLETE WAVE Sonja Shaw, a candidate for California superintendent of public instruction who has been involved in filing federal civil rights complaints over transgender athlete policies, also sharply criticized the dismissal. "Parents in California are no strangers to this fight, or to these underhanded tactics. We stood up to Gavin Newsom and the CIF when they decided girls’ sports and girls’ locker rooms were political fodder," she said. "A Biden-appointed judge just tossed out a case that should have protected female athletes, and she did it after the Supreme Court already ruled that states can keep women’s teams as a safe space for biological females. That is a political choice dressed up as law, and it is the girls who get robbed." "This fight is not going away, and neither am I," Shaw continued. "I am not backing down because an activist judge in a kangaroo court dismissed a case. This is a hill we are willing to die on. We will keep fighting for fairness, safety, privacy and the future of female athletes. California parents have been told 'no' before, and we refused to quit then. We’re not quitting now. We will keep standing, we will keep fighting, and we will keep protecting our girls." SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS The California Interscholastic Federation declined to weigh in on the court’s dismissal when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday. "The CIF does not comment on legal matters," CIF Director of Media Rebecca Brutlag said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The California Department of Education also declined to address the substance of the ruling when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday, citing the ongoing legal proceedings. "The California Department of Education cannot comment on pending litigation," a CDE spokesperson said. The legal fight intensified after transgender Jurupa Valley High School athlete AB Hernandez won girls’ events at California’s state track championships, prompting federal scrutiny and changes by the CIF intended to preserve qualifying and podium positions for biological female athletes. news.summary: The Justice Department is weighing an appeal after a federal judge dismissed Trump's lawsuit over transgender athletes in California girls' sports.

news.title: Canada’s trade surplus plummeted in July, before US tariffs
news.text:
Canada's trade surplus with the US was nearly halved to C$5.9 billion in July, down from C$10.3 billion in June. (EPA Images pic)
MONTREAL: Canada's trade surplus declined sharply in July as the price of oil and precious metals fell, the national statistics agency said Thursday, with US tariffs imposed since then expected to add further pressure on exports.
The trade surplus in July was C$769 million (US$558 million), down from C$4.2 billion (US$3.1 billion) the month prior, Statistics Canada said.
Exports to the US - where much of Canada's crude goes - fell by 6.6% in July, "the strongest percentage decrease since April 2025," the agency said.
The trade surplus with the US was nearly halved to C$5.9 billion in July, down from C$10.3 billion in June.
Trade talks between the US and Canada broke down late last month, with US President Donald Trump's threatened tariffs of up to 50% since coming into force.
Canada has announced retaliatory measures, set to take effect next week.
The trade war is expected to weigh on trade between the neighbors, with Ottawa additionally urging consumers to prioritize Canadian products.
news.summary: Exports to the US fell by 6.6%, the sharpest percentage decline since April 2025.
